t: Two thousand twenty-six was supposed to be the year of agents. And honestly? It delivered. From OpenClot at the start of the year to platforms like Muse, GrokBot and Instinct, autonomous agents are quietly doing huge chunks of people's work.
Right. We went from agents being the next big thing to just... being here.
But here's the catch. Most of our work isn't done alone. We work in teams. And almost every agent so far has been a solo affair — it only covers the part of your job you do by yourself.
Which is why today's conversation is all about team agents — shared, multiplayer AI that lives between people. It's an operator's cut with Nufar Gaspar on the AI Daily Brief.
She opened with two stories you will absolutely recognize. Story one: the person who can't take a vacation.
Oh, every company has one.

The one who knows how pricing exceptions work, or how the biggest customer was configured three years ago. When they're swamped, work waits. When they're on vacation, someone calls them. And when they leave, a piece of the company leaves with them.
And she said one company she works with has a person like that for every domain. Nobody takes vacation without getting a call.
Story two: work that nobody fully owns. A customer moves from sales to marketing to customer success.
Sales made promises in the deal, marketing runs different messaging, and success finds out about the promises weeks before renewal. Everyone has a piece. Nobody has the picture.
And the kicker — even if each team is using AI, those agents don't talk to each other. Siloed agents often make it worse.
So what's the pattern at the AI-forward companies? She says it plays out in three steps.

Step one: everybody builds their own agents and loves the productivity boost. Step two: agent sprawl — lots of overlapping work, each agent maintained by one person, each dying the day its owner loses interest or leaves.
And step three: they merge into team-level agents. Fewer agents, much broader scope, each with a named owner.
And this is public. Every gave every employee an agent early in the year and moved to shared team agents by May. Sierra merged its specialist agents into one. Shopify runs an internal team agent.
Okay, so definitions. Multiplayer AI, shared agents, AI teammates, company brain — it's all the same thing. Her working definition?
One agent that many people talk to, with shared knowledge, shared memory, and one configuration. The instructions, skills, access, and owner are all shared.
Not the same as a skill library, though.

Right. A skill is a playbook for a specific task. A team agent works across a diverse set of tasks, carries the team's knowledge, and remembers what it learns. A skill library is one ingredient, not the whole dish.
Now — important nuance. Not every agent should be shared. She laid out a dial with three settings.
Setting one: fully private agents. Her own social media agent stays private — nobody else should ever sound like her, she says.

Setting two: shared knowledge, private agents. Every salesperson keeps their own prospecting agent with their own voice, but they all point at the same well-maintained picture of the ideal customer and messaging.
That hybrid is often the right answer and the easiest place to start. Setting three: the full team agent — one agent, many people, its own job, its own owner.
And agents can move along the dial. If your colleagues keep asking to borrow your private agent, that's the sign.
So team agents come in four archetypes. First, the expert agent — one person's know-how made available to everyone.
That's the vacation-person problem, solved. Think a data agent that answers any data question across departments, or a pricing and deal desk agent, or compliance.

To get it right, the knowledge has to come from the experts themselves — interview them, harvest answers they've already given. And involve them from day one. For them it's the vacation finally made possible...
...and also a lot of job insecurity. Tread carefully.
Second archetype: the common work agent. Many people doing similar recurring work, one shared way to do it. You recognize it when three people have each built their own version of the same agent.

Classic examples: team research and meeting prep, or a marketing team's content agent. Getting it right means agreeing on how the work is done — merging the best of three versions is really a conversation about standards.
Third: the bridge agent. Work that flows between roles where nobody can do it alone. You recognize it when the handoffs break.
Like a customer agent spanning sales, solutions, customer success, and delivery. Each function feeds in its own piece — and permissions need very careful attention.

And fourth: the chief of staff. It owns the team's day-to-day operations — decisions, commitments, status, onboarding. You recognize it when the team keeps repeating itself and new joiners take weeks to find their footing.
Okay, but she also gave a reality check. Three signs a team agent is the wrong move — at least for now.

One: taste beats standards. If people truly need different answers or their own voice is the point, keep those agents private. Two: nobody can own the knowledge — if no one will maintain it, the agent drifts within weeks, sometimes days.
Three: if a shared agent complicates more than it simplifies — conflicting needs, tangled permissions, endless coordination — just don't. Not until you've untangled it.
And notice what's not on the list: sensitive data and high stakes. Those aren't reasons against — they're design questions.

Which brings us to the playbook: five design decisions. And she runs one example the whole way through — a customer agent, the bridge kind, holding everything the company knows about each customer and everything promised them.

Decision one: what it does. Write down who it serves, by role — sales asks different things than delivery. Give it a broad area of work: meeting prep, where do we stand, flag promises that commit other teams, draft every handoff.

But don't skip the don'ts list. It never makes commitments on someone's behalf. Never settles disagreements between people — that goes to the owner. Never carries information from a private space into a shared one, and never discusses one customer in another customer's space.
And start narrow — reading and drafting first. Expand the scope only as it earns trust.

Decision two: where it lives. Three options, simplest to most involved. A shared folder everyone points their own tools at. A vendor-hosted agent — Claude Tag, ChatGPT's Workspace Agent, Copilot, Notion. Or self-hosted — open source like OpenClaw or Hermes on your own servers, or a custom harness.
Two questions come with that. Who can see each person's conversations with the agent? In Claude in Slack, everyone in the channel sees — and can even steer it. Other tools keep chats private.

And where does its learning live — per person, per channel, or one shared memory for the whole workspace? Never across customers. Her rule: pick the simplest option two people will actually use this week.
Decision three — arguably the most important: what it knows. This is where the team agrees on ground truth. Which definitions, which version of the pricing policy is the real one.
She says that conversation is worth having even if you never ship the agent.
Four stages. Collect — interview the knowledge holders, harvest what's already written, let AI do the heavy lifting. Refine — merge, surface the contradictions...
...and you will find five versions of the truth.

Date everything, and keep out passwords, notes about people, one customer's details in another's space. Approve — each piece signed off by its owner. And maintain — decide what the agent may add to its own memory versus what needs a human review, and put the upkeep on a schedule.
Decision four: what it can touch. Your own agent acts as you. A team agent acts for many people. First rule — whose access does it use?

Act as whoever's asking — safest, and right when people have different access levels. Or give it its own account with exactly the access the job needs. Using one person's login? Read-only, non-sensitive only — and honestly, she wouldn't recommend it at all.
Second rule: who can ask it. Drop an agent with pricing-sheet access into a channel of forty people — including a few contractors — and suddenly all forty can get the pricing just by asking.

Third: where the answer lands. This one runs the other way. The asker has every right to the answer, but it can surface in a shared space in front of people who don't. Claude in Slack uses the asker's connections, and the docs note it doesn't consider who else is in the channel. Sensitive answers go privately.
And keep a record of who asked for what — because when the agent works under its own account, the logs just say the agent did it.
Decision five: how you run it. One owner — one person or a very small group who owns priorities and decides what happens when two people ask for opposite things.
Clear rules of engagement — what it does, what it doesn't, who sees your conversation, how to correct it. People trust an agent more when they understand what it's learning.

Put decisions where it can see them. If the team decides things in DMs and hallway conversations, the agent never hears about it. And keep watching — start with a small pilot, keep test questions you can rerun, and be ready to retire it.
A few closing thoughts from the Q&A. Which archetype do teams actually start with? Not the bridge — it sounds the most attractive but it's the hardest to execute.

The expert agents are the lowest-hanging fruit. They create good redundancy and relieve the bottlenecks. And NLW made the point that the agentified internal knowledge base — company policies through a chatbot — was the OG team agent before anyone had the vocabulary.
And build-versus-wait? Why invest before Copilot or OpenAI just drops a native version?

Because the heavy lifting is always the configuration and the knowledge curation. Pick the tool closest to your existing ecosystem. Even a naive implementation future-proofs you — you've already agreed on the ground truth. And don't build your own Claude Tag. Your moat is everything those companies can't tap into.

Final thought from her: everything covered holds no matter what ships next, because the decisions are orthogonal to any specific tool. Expect more formalization around identity, permissions, and ownership through the rest of the year.
That's the playbook. Four archetypes, three signs to wait, five design decisions — and one dial to decide whether the agent stays yours.
